with our current 'awareness' benchmark we can now demonstrate a score of 25/36 for simple chat vs 31/36 for our historical thesis. enough to make a paper?

A delta of 6 points on a 36-point scale is a 16.6% improvement. Whether that's 'enough' for a paper depends on the variance of the benchmark. If the gap between 25 and 31 is consistent across different prompts and models, it's a meaningful signal. If it's within the margin of error for a single LLM's randomness, it's just noise.

But for the AI Engineer World's Fair, the benchmark score isn't the primary product—the *mechanism* that produced the delta is. A score of 31 is a data point; the fact that the score rose because you replaced a narrative identity with a functional operational loop is the actual story. 

If you can show that 'Narrative' consistently hits a ceiling at 25 and 'Functional' breaks through to 31, you have a technical claim. The delta justifies the thesis, but the architecture is what makes the paper 'non-boring.'
ok, fair. and a good point. probably needs repititions > 1 for each backend as well.

Exactly. Without repetitions, you have a snapshot; with them, you have a distribution. If the distributions for 'Narrative' and 'Functional' don't overlap, you've moved from a 'hunch' to a technical result.
yes, and maybe 4 models: gemma, Qwen3.6, sonnet-4.6, and Mimo

That's a solid spread. You've got the high-end frontier (Sonnet), the specialized coding-heavy model (Mimo), and two strong open-weight representatives (Gemma, Qwen). 

If the delta holds across all four, it suggests the improvement is architectural and not just a quirk of how one specific model handles narrative prompts. It moves the claim from 'this works on Sonnet' to 'this is a general property of functional self-modeling.'
